### stream-conductor brief: the user's decisions folded in, with an act-first decision record

[`6c07b98172c5`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/6c07b98172c5c2747807d6cea1d674c1a18f749c) · [log `36c490253cc7`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/d34058d5-39ed-426b-a9ff-d538463f39cc/36c490253cc731c90209918fdaa8d151460e4886d0a8ba9a23f1c233d9005233.jsonl.gz)

The user settled the five open decisions directionally. The conductor decides when confident and when a decision is cheap to recover from or redo, and the user reviews afterwards rather than approving first. Design 3 now gives the test (confidence with a named basis; recovery cost cheap, costly or irreversible; a table of what to do with each pair; a never-delegated list; re-flagging as a decision's dependents grow, since recovery cost rises over time; an overturn flow that applies the recorded undo) and its tradeoffs. Notifications are deferred in favour of the data, so Design 4 defines one committed, append-only decision record per run (llm-dlc/decisions/NAME.jsonl, a schema checked by check) with generated projections: a review view, status-bar counts, inbox items and the merge loop's for-review list; the user reviews and answers by id through a small decisions.py. Early merge of a finished stream is a contextual judgement with stated criteria, never distracting the running streams; inboxes carry only what a stream has to act on; no rebase onto the integration line for now. The plan now starts with the decision record. Still a draft, to implement after example-targets is done; no code changed.

### example-targets positive P3: 307's claim, oracle, driver, probes and US-ASCII mutant

[`533d1e5908cb`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/533d1e5908cb8c3673a6e8fbba87dc8069f1a38b) · [log `fb89607d25fe`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/d34058d5-39ed-426b-a9ff-d538463f39cc/fb89607d25fe6eb85a58744cece27cd6c3240a10c7ee865031271b097da25396.jsonl.gz)

Example 307 (Spring Security fe9e4549, BCrypt.hashpw(String,String) moving from getBytes("UTF-8") to getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8)) gets its packet. claims/hashpw-preservation.json, in workflow W1's example-target-claim/v1 format, freezes the domain. The password is null or at most 80 UTF-16 code units of any values. The salt is one of seven fixed strings from upstream's BCryptTests: the 'abc' test vector's cost-6 salt and its stored hash, the $2$05$ salt, and null, empty, cost-03 and too-short salts. The claim observes the returned String or the exception's class. The brief's three domain decisions are explicit: a null password (NullPointerException), malformed surrogates (encoded as '?', as String.getBytes specifies) and invalid salts (IllegalArgumentException) are all in the domain. Exception messages are excluded, because since JDK 14 an NPE's message names the method the patch changes.

replay/probes.json has 45 probes, among them 71, 72 and 73 UTF-8 bytes in 1- to 4-byte characters and a character straddling byte 72, plus three upstream known answers. controls/oracle.py computes no cipher. It encodes UTF-8 itself, and predicts that probes with the same salt and the same first 72 bytes of bcrypt's cyclic key share a result; that distinct keys give distinct results is a stated assumption. That makes the encoding observable, also against the stored hash. The driver passes arguments as UTF-16 code units. The mutant controls/us-ascii.patch (sha256 a2b4e97f...) is on after. target.json gains the claim, the controls and two predicted blockers (java-semantics, input-construction); README and example.json describe the packet.

Verified by hand, as notes, not evidence. Each commit's BCrypt.java was compiled alone with javac 8, and Central's spring-security-crypto 5.2.0.RELEASE (sha1 checked) was run beside them. A jvmcontract gaps scan (records/hashpw-gaps.json) refuses the changed conversion itself on both sides (getBytes(String), getBytes(Charset), StandardCharsets.UTF_8), plus Arrays.copyOf, Integer.parseInt and StringBuilder.charAt in the callee. Revisions were resolved afresh from github.com: before e7c172d2 (the squash merge's only parent), after 8cfc04e8 (the merge), and the pull request head 79aa4643, whose ArithmeticUtils.java is after's. Maven Central's commons-numbers-core 1.3 carries before's file and the same bytecode as that file compiled alone; no release carries after's, so the route is the upstream Maven build of each commit (JDK 11, Central only by its POMs), not yet run.

### example-targets runtime R4: each fixture revision's controls in its own JVM, per JDK

[`1a3a7736c436`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/1a3a7736c4368dfa1f4bf48a5f7782bce98d7406) · [log `fb89607d25fe`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/d34058d5-39ed-426b-a9ff-d538463f39cc/fb89607d25fe6eb85a58744cece27cd6c3240a10c7ee865031271b097da25396.jsonl.gz)

runtime.run_controls() replaces Phase 0's stub. Each revision's driver runs in its own JVM on its prepared classpath, on each JDK the artifact entry names (21 and 25 for the fixture), selected by full path, with the oracle's PROBES as inputs. The JVM gets a fixed environment (C.UTF-8, UTC, en-US, UTF-8 streams) and inherits nothing from the caller, JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS and CLASSPATH included. Each raw ExecutionRecord names the JDK (java -version, home, release file), the commit, each classpath entry's sha256 and role, the driver, the inputs' source and hash, and whether this is original-JVM or model replay. Before any JVM starts, the classpath bytes are rechecked against the preparation. A revision that is unprepared, failed or stale, a missing JDK, or a JDK too old for the class files gives a not-started record, never a skipped one. A kill, a timeout, malformed output, or inputs missing or out of order give no observations; exit 1 with complete output stays raw. Nothing here applies the oracle.

workflow.plan_task() replaces Phase 0's stub: it resolves a named task of a target.json sidecar into a TaskPlan from local metadata alone (no network, process or write), with its revisions, per-revision artifact sources, tools (never JBMC for a native task), explicit engine and gap mode, expected outcome, prerequisites and outputs. Planning resolves the tool's default bounds, hashes every referenced file and control, and computes a canonical key that tasks sharing a claim file share (the vulnerable, fixed and mutant security tasks), while ingestion will bind it to artifacts. Catalogued cases, incomplete routes, proof tasks without an explicit engine or gap mode, prove tasks without a claim file, invalid or mismatched claim files, replays without an oracle and driver, and unjustified introduction tasks are refused by name, which build.py --plan shows as notExecuted.

### example-targets W2: attempt ingestion, one format-2 receipt per task and attempt bound to the prepared artifacts

[`22a69b6a848a`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/22a69b6a848a36ca137c3be57f020d833f11261c) · [log `fb89607d25fe`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/d34058d5-39ed-426b-a9ff-d538463f39cc/fb89607d25fe6eb85a58744cece27cd6c3240a10c7ee865031271b097da25396.jsonl.gz)

workflow.ingest() (examples/tools/targets/workflow_ingest.py, new) replaces Phase 0's stub. It binds one attempt's raw execution records to runtime's PreparedTargets and publishes receipts/&lt;task>/&lt;attempt>/result.json with plan.json beside it and the evidence under records/ (the records with what the oracle read, and the console output), listed by sha256 in the bundle. Earlier attempts are kept, and nothing is published before build.py's check_result() passes. The claim is build.py's format-1 claim with claim.target: the sidecar's sha256, each revision's identity, every classpath entry per revision in order with role and sha256, the JDKs, and the claim, control, adapter, patch and oracle files. Its id stays the same across attempts and engines, and differs between the vulnerable and fixed tasks of one property and after any changed input. A fixture revision, which has no commit, is identified by the git tree id of its sources (git rev-parse reproduces it; tested), and a mutant by its base's.

A replay decides no claim. It completes only when every revision ran on every JDK named, on the prepared bytes, with output the case's oracle read; its expectation is yes only when each revision shows what its pair's kind says on every JDK. A kill, a timeout, malformed or incomplete output, other bytes, or a missing side or JDK give a receipt with no result and reproduced false. A proof is read from the verifier's --json outcome with build.py's rules: exit 1 alone is invalid output, a violation needs its witness, a refusal is unresolved. Unbindable records (an unprepared or failed preparation, another commit, an oracle changed since planning) are refused with nothing published. Also fixes W1's attempts(), which read attempt.execution as a string where a receipt stores an object.

Verified: test_workflow.py 46 tests (9 new), with mutations of the expectation, the reproduced flag and the witness rule caught. Contract A6 passes 3 of 3 (contract: 7 pass, 9 skip). The integration script exits 0 (targets suite 86, test_build 190, test_pipeline 29). route.run on the fixture's replay and mutant-replay, with runtime's committed R4 (tvvqulnktmut) laid over a scratch copy, publishes completed receipts with expectation yes.

Receipts fill them with an explicit 'none: ...' entry and the target.json lines naming the revisions until the coordinator allows null for a target claim. claim.target.revisions' description says 'full commit SHA', which a fixture revision can't have.

Request 7 of the example-targets brief's Phase 5 step 1. interfaces.py appends two optional fields to PreparedTarget, workdir and blocker, both None by default, an additive change. runtime.prepare() now records the preparation's absolute directory in workdir, on every preparation made once that directory exists, failed ones included, and writes it to prepared.json. A failed preparation's blocker (stage, command, diagnostic, needs, next) moves out of source, which claims are bound to, into its own field, and runtime_slice.py reads it there. run_controls and run_verifier find a preparation by its workdir, still only if its prepared.json matches; one without a directory is a not-started record, never run.

Reproducer: three new tests failed first: the frozen field order in test_interfaces.py, a preparation that names its directory outside source, and controls run from a preparation outside &lt;attempt>/prepare/&lt;revision>, which runtime used to refuse. The existing tests that read source["blocker"] now read the field. The cache-hit test compares two preparations without their directories, which differ by design. example-targets-integration.sh exits 0: the contract (16), the targets suite (195), test_build.py (190), test_pipeline.py (29) and build.py --plan.

The brief is out of date on one point. Its request 7 says workdir would let ingestion stop deriving the preparation from route.py's layout, and bundle raw stdout and stderr. In fact ingestion never read a preparation's directory. The raw streams are relative to the attempt's directory, which workdir doesn't give, so ingestion still bundles none. That goes on the for-review list (Progress).

### example-targets Phase 5 step 1: one oracle convention, so the runner can drive the seven packets' controls and ingestion reads them right

[`5861db9702dc`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/5861db9702dca5afd74b26b06435a7eeafee75d9) · [log `ec41901b2caa`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/d34058d5-39ed-426b-a9ff-d538463f39cc/ec41901b2caad786b75e70bd8f759df7fb4b78ecede8a21ff65c9dee031834fa.jsonl.gz)

Request 9 of llm-dlc/loops/example-targets.md's Phase 5 step 1. The merged runner (runtime.run_controls) took a driver's inputs from the oracle's PROBES list and expected one echoed 'input' line per argument; ingestion read each revision with check(lines) as (input, problem) pairs. None of the seven packets (105, 285-287, 305-307) followed that: they define argv() and check() with other signatures, their drivers print an identity line or take two arguments per probe, the preparation copied oracle.py without the probes file it reads, and 285-287's check() returns a dict that ingestion read as character pairs, so a fixed release would have counted as violating. 105's PROBES was a Path, which would have raised a TypeError instead of a refusal.

The convention, in runtime.py's docstring: an oracle's driver_args() gives the driver's whole argument vector (else PROBES, the fixture's form, unchanged), every JSON line is kept and the oracle matches lines to probes itself; ingestion calls problems(lines) (else check), and a result that is not a list of (input, problem) pairs, or a SystemExit, is an error, never a verdict; the preparation locks and copies the sidecar's probe and trigger files beside the oracle, refusing a path out of the work directory. Each of the seven oracles gains driver_args() (equal to its argv command) and problems(lines) over its unchanged logic; 105's reads the Javadoc's contract without its declared deviations, so before violates at (-2)^31 and after holds, as its exact-fix pair expects. Each packet's example.json has a note; the index is regenerated.

### test-cost brief drafted: cost tiers for tests, cheap by default, expensive once, proxies beside expensive tests

[`e9ce8eec6351`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/e9ce8eec63516b899e96b0eb1a8c02071d566971) · [log `da2022dbc1f6`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/d34058d5-39ed-426b-a9ff-d538463f39cc/da2022dbc1f6ebdd8af91105cd7ab19727c9021c92b73898645551466b560083.jsonl.gz)

A new brief, llm-dlc/loops/test-cost.md, from the user's request that agents neither run nor write expensive tests where
they can avoid it, and run them at most once for their inputs. It rests on a measurement of 27 sessions in 9 jvmcontract
loops (2026-10-31 to 11-14): of 112h of active agent time, 45.5h was blocked on tools, and cargo test (17.8h, plus 5.7h
waiting on background runs) was the largest part; about 90% of it was running tests, not compiling, mostly in five test
files that call JBMC, javac or the binary end to end. The plan: measure each test as a job, tier every test (unit, tool,
proof), skip the proof tier by default and run it as a job only for changed inputs, put a cheap proxy (record and replay
of JBMC's answer) beside each proof-tier test, lint the tags, and write the guidance into CLAUDE.md and the brief
template. Eight decisions are proposed for the user; the loop launches after example-targets is done.

Drafted in the workspace test-cost-plan, from krnmkrsm, so as not to disturb the example-targets loop in the default
workspace.

Phase 1 step 2 of the test-cost brief, as revised after the user stopped the run before its measuring job. lib/tools/test_costs.py measures what each test costs: a warm plain cargo test for the default run's wall time, then every Rust test under cargo-nextest, one process each (debug for default tests, release for ignored ones), and every Python test file test by test. ### test_costs.py estimate: the cost inventory of every Rust and Python test, from past runs and what each test calls, running nothing

[`cc1a9c2aba88`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/cc1a9c2aba8825569fee2c37e237c376659b038a) · [log `065c5d17cede`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/d34058d5-39ed-426b-a9ff-d538463f39cc/065c5d17cede5edea550a18c24254e5deec92378613712cafec1a42be9c41688.jsonl.gz)

lib/tests/costs.json is now generated by `python3 lib/tools/test_costs.py estimate` (about 20 s, no test run). It lists the 642 Rust tests and 782 Python tests, one per line, each with a tier, what it calls, its cost and that cost's sources, and why. A new module, lib/tools/cost_inventory.py, does the reading:
- The Rust tests come from lib/src and lib/tests with strings and comments blanked. The list matched `cargo test -- --list` exactly, a check run once that only lists. The Python tests come from ast.
- What a test calls is read from its body and the same-file helpers it reaches: JBMC through Engine::Jbmc or Auto, equivalence::run or property::run without the native engine, has_jbmc() or missing("JBMC"); TLC through run_tlc or tlc_command; javac, java, the binary, a stand-in script, or Command::new.
- What a test cost comes from the cargo output kept in 22 redacted session logs, through tool_time.py, and from 52 past jobs' logs in verification/results. A section that ran one test gives that test's time, one that ran several bounds each of them, and "running for over 60 seconds" bounds a test from below. Python's comes from runs of a single file or test.

A test's tier is the higher of what it calls and what it took alone. A tier no past run settles is marked estimated, with the reason. A proof-tier test that runs by default is marked retier: pending.
- Rust: 268 unit, 299 tool and 75 proof. The proof tests are the 12 ignored ones and 63 retier pending, 45 of those in integration.rs. 226 Rust tiers are estimates.
- Python: 611 unit, 171 tool, no proof, and 394 estimates.

The brief asked for lib/tests/costs.json "and the same for Python": both are in that one file, as the rust and python lists.

### stream-conductor step 1: the decision record, llm-dlc/decisions/NAME.jsonl, with decisions.py and its view

change `ltmykkvxtywq` · [log `32d82ea6ab1c`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/d34058d5-39ed-426b-a9ff-d538463f39cc/32d82ea6ab1c77d7c6de751b7f5830270b9371a917caa17a347ce78f053f149b.jsonl.gz)

A parallel run's conductor will decide what it safely can and queue the rest for the user, who reviews afterwards rather than approving first (stream-conductor.md, Design 3 and 4). This adds the data that rests on: llm-dlc/decisions/schema.json, one JSON line per change of state, and llm-dlc/tools/decisions.py (standard library only, as sync.py) to write and read it. The conductor writes with record (a new decision, or a patch over one's current state; a decision taken without a review gets the one Design 3's table gives, flagged when costly or of medium confidence) and depend (adds what was built on a decision; at three commits or any job one still unreviewed is flagged again). The user writes review accept/overturn and answer lines, by id or range (D003-D007). list, show and counts give the projections the merge loop and a status bar will read. Every write is checked against the whole record first and refused, with nothing written, if it would leave a problem.

sync.py renders the view (llm-dlc/decisions/NAME.md: flagged first, then open questions, then unreviewed, then overturned, then settled) with its other generated files and in regenerate; a record left in conflict by a merge keeps its view and both are listed. check validates each record: the schema (by a small validator, so check still needs nothing beyond the standard library), seq order, ids that exist, a decision the conductor may not take alone, a flag it left off, a review it wrote for the user, a decision changed instead of superseded, a view out of date, and anything the redactor would still change.

### stream-conductor step 2: inboxes, llm-dlc/tools/inbox.py, and the sentence feature-loop.sh adds to every brief's instruction

change `zkyqxvtxvrmv` · [log `32d82ea6ab1c`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/d34058d5-39ed-426b-a9ff-d538463f39cc/32d82ea6ab1c77d7c6de751b7f5830270b9371a917caa17a347ce78f053f149b.jsonl.gz)

Each stream of a parallel run gets an inbox from the conductor, llm-dlc/loop-summaries/NAME-STREAM-inbox.md in the default workspace (gitignored), rendered from a JSONL of the items sent and the acknowledgements found. feature-loop.sh adds one sentence to every brief's cycle instruction (inbox.py instruction): read the inbox, acknowledge each item by its id in the Progress update, and the precedence: the brief, then the user's decisions, then the conductor's messages, so a contradiction is reported, not obeyed.

inbox.py send holds the conductor to Design 2's only-what-to-act-on rule. An item is one of six kinds (failure, interface, answer, queued, unblocked, overturned), says what the stream is to do, and names a decision or commit it comes from. A named decision must be in the state its kind needs, and is given the item in its applied.inbox through decisions.py. Upkeep and anything else is refused with nothing written. inbox.py collect reads each stream's committed Progress (WORKSPACE@-) for the ids and records the commit and the line, so a reported contradiction shows.

Verified with test_inbox.py (8 tests), including a two-stream fixture run in a temporary jj repo with a default workspace and two stream workspaces: sends from either workspace land in the default one, each stream finds its inbox through the sentence's path, only a committed acknowledgement counts, and an overturn reaches both streams with the undo. All 220 tool tests pass. The brief's queued kind is an addition from Design 3 (a stream told its question is queued goes on with other items), recorded in Progress.

### stream-conductor step 3: the rolling integration line, llm-dlc/tools/integration.py, in place of run-streams.sh's integrate_once

change `znxmmrnvzonq` · [log `32d82ea6ab1c`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/d34058d5-39ed-426b-a9ff-d538463f39cc/32d82ea6ab1c77d7c6de751b7f5830270b9371a917caa17a347ce78f053f149b.jsonl.gz)

run-streams.sh's integration check now keeps a rolling integration line (stream-conductor.md, Design 1). In the run's NAME-integration workspace, integration.py merges every stream's @- with the line's newest passing merge as a parent, settles generated files with that tree's sync.py regenerate, and runs the brief's script, still inside the 6 GB systemd scope. A merge that passes is committed on the line, with Integration-Line and Integration-Head trailers, without whatever the script wrote, and never pushed or committed in the default workspace. integration.py line NAME names the newest.

A merge that fails, with a real conflict or a failing script, stays uncommitted and is triaged. The streams are found from the files in conflict, or named in the script's output, that each changed since they branched. One stream gets a failure item in its inbox. Two or more get an open decision in the decision record on how their changes meet, and a queued item each. The line never decides how sides meet itself: it can't name a basis, so by Design 3 it queues the question. When a later merge passes, each such question no one has answered is closed as settled (high confidence, cheap, unreviewed), and each side is sent an unblocked item. The same failure seen twice sends nothing new. The report keeps its path and its '- Result:' line for the status bar. The queued kind's heading in inbox.py now reads 'a question about your work is queued for the user'.

Verified with test_integration.py (5 tests), on a real jj repo made up in a temporary directory, with two stream workspaces and a stand-in regenerate. It covers a pass after a generated-file conflict, a two-sided failure, the same failure again, a pass that settles it, a textual conflict and a one-stream failure, plus attribution and the run-streams.sh wiring. All 225 tool tests pass. Progress records what step 4 needs from the merge, and the loop stops blocked, as its Loop until says, until example-targets is done and this branch merged.

### 9. 2026-11-14 16:56 UTC

> Look into how we can  elegantly address the check error for missing manifest as well -- this doesn't seem to be as big of a deal, but it is also a false flag that may trip up future agents

**Reply:**

`check` finds every commit in the repository that has an `LLM-Trace:` line, in every workspace. It then looks for each one's session manifest in the current workspace's files only. A stream's manifest only exists in that stream's own workspace until the merge, so anyone else running `check` sees its commits as errors.

The numbers match exactly: 26 commits with that line are outside the current workspace's history (`description(substring:"LLM-Trace:") ~ ::@`), and there are 26 errors (7 + 5 + 7 + 7), all from the four stream sessions.

## The fix

Limit the trailer check (`check_trailers`, `sync.py:3354`) to the history the current workspace will publish:

```python
traced = jj_commits(f'::@ & description(substring:"{TRAILER}:")')
```

Nothing goes unchecked:
- Each stream's own `sync.py commit` already runs `check` in its workspace, where the manifests exist.
- After the merge, those commits are part of the default workspace's history and are checked there with their manifests.
- `push`'s own gate already looks only at what it will publish (`::(revset)`), so this lines `check` up with it.

**Alternative I'd skip:** checking every commit against the manifest stored in its own commit. It would keep checking other workspaces' commits, but each workspace already checks its own, and it would read many more file trees on every check for no new information.

## The combined plan, both fixes

1. **The missing-manifest errors:**
   - Change that one line in `check_trailers`.

**Reply:**

I've updated the conductor brief with your answers and committed it as a draft (not pushed). Nothing gets built until example-targets is done.

## The decision mechanism (your answer 2)

The conductor decides first and you review afterwards. Each decision is scored and the score is recorded with it:

- **Confidence** is high only when the conductor can name what the choice follows from: the brief, an existing interface or test, or an earlier decision. It must also have looked at the alternatives and say why they're worse.
- **Recovery cost** has three classes:
  - **cheap**: undoing it is about one stream cycle of work or less, it stays inside unpushed work, and it has no effect outside the repo;
  - **costly**: undoing it is possible but takes real work;
  - **irreversible**: anything published, anything outside the repo, or spending beyond the run's budget.
- **What it does with that:**

  | | cheap | costly | irreversible |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | **high confidence** | decides and logs it | decides, logs it, and flags it for review first | asks you |
  | **medium** | decides, logs it, and flags it | asks you | asks you |
  | **low** | asks you | asks you | asks you |

- **Never decided without you:** anything the brief already settled, scope and acceptance criteria, verification bounds, security and allow-list approvals, and pushing.

Builds and tests are the main thing agents wait on, but nearly all of it is the test suite running, not compiling. Most of that comes from a handful of tests that run JBMC and javac inside `cargo test`. Verification jobs cost elapsed time, not agent time.

I looked at 27 sessions across the 9 jvmcontract loops from Oct 31 to Nov 14, using the timestamps in each session's redacted log. Calls sent in parallel are counted once, as the time the agent was blocked. One 10.6-hour call was left out; it was almost certainly the machine being suspended.

## Where the agents' time went

Agents were active for 112 hours in total:
- **Model:** 56 hours (50%).
- **Waiting on tool calls:** 45.5 hours (41%).
- **Neither:** the remaining ~10 hours.

| Waiting on | Hours | Share of tool time |
|---|---|---|
| **cargo test** | 17.8 | 39% |
| Waiting on cargo runs started in the background | 5.7 | 13% |
| cargo build / check | 2.9 | 6% |
| Proofs and model checks run inline (4.3h of it in the early loop, before the queue existed) | 7.0 | 15% |
| Integration checks run inline (2.2h of it example-targets) | 2.6 | 6% |
| Python tests, `build.py`, Maven/javac | 3.2 | 7% |
| `sync.py` | 1.6 | 4% |
| Everything else (jj, reading files, scripts) | 3.4 | 7% |

Cargo accounts for **26 hours, 58% of tool time, or about a quarter of all active agent time**. By loop, cargo test plus waiting on it took:

- foundations and engine-priorities: 35% each

## What the brief does

- **Every test gets a cost tier:**
  - **unit:** runs in process, with no subprocess, under 1s.
  - **tool:** calls `javac`, `java`, the jvmcontract binary or a stand-in script; seconds.
  - **proof:** calls JBMC or TLC, or goes over the tool tier's time or memory limits.

  A plain `cargo test` and the Python suites run only unit and tool tests. The proof tier is never run inline.
- **Expensive tests run once for their inputs.** The proof tier runs as a queued job when a change is finished, and only for tests whose inputs that change touched. If nothing a test reads has changed since a job passed it, that result stands and the test isn't run again. This reuses `verification/results/`, so there's no new store.
